questions.scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration: the review prompt contains the rule "NEVER comment on files under /generated." The reviewer obeys it, but it still posts findings on machine-generated API stubs in /api/stubs and on a vendored copy of an open-source library in /third_party. Developers cannot edit those files and dismiss every such finding. New folders of this kind appear every few weeks, so keeping a hand-made folder list up to date has not worked.
questions.stem: Which prompt change will MOST reliably stop these findings without hiding issues in code the team writes itself?

options.text: Rewrite the rule as "CRITICAL: NEVER comment on ANY generated code, NO EXCEPTIONS" in capitals so the reviewer treats it as its top-priority instruction.
Tell the reviewer to skip any file it is unsure the team wrote, so that borderline or ambiguous files produce no findings at all.
Explain why the rule exists (developers can act only on hand-written code) and say to skip generated or vendored files marked "do not edit".
Add the two new folders to the rule's exclusion list, and ask developers to report any other folders that need excluding as they come up.

questions.explanation: The bare rule names one folder, so the model applies it literally to that folder and nowhere else. Anthropic recommends giving the context or motivation behind an instruction, because Claude can then generalize from the explanation. Stating the purpose (findings only help on code people edit by hand) plus a recognizable test (generated or vendored files, "do not edit" headers) lets the reviewer skip new folders of the same kind while still reviewing everything the team writes.

whyWrong.A: Shouting the rule does not explain what counts as generated, and still says nothing about vendored code. Anthropic also notes that aggressive wording can make current models over-trigger, which here could mean skipping real code.
whyWrong.B: This trades false positives for missed issues: any hand-written file the model is unsure about would go unreviewed, which the team explicitly wants to avoid.
whyWrong.D: This is the same hand-made list that has already failed; it fixes today's two folders and breaks again when the next one appears.

questions.mindset: Tell the model why a rule exists so it can apply the intent to cases you did not list.

questions.stem: An online retailer uses Claude to moderate product reviews before they are published. The prompt says: "Remove reviews that are inappropriate." The merchandising team finds that many honest one-star reviews describing a broken product are being removed, which customers notice and complain about. The team wants fewer wrongful removals without letting abusive content through. What is the BEST change to the prompt?

options.text: List the removal reasons (profanity, personal data, spam links, off-topic content) and state that negative opinions about the product are allowed.
Tell Claude to remove a review only when it is very confident the review is inappropriate and to keep it whenever it is in any doubt at all.
Ask Claude to rate each review's negativity from 1 to 10 and automatically publish only reviews that score below a threshold the merchandising team sets.
Add a role line telling Claude it is a fair and balanced community manager who respects customers' freedom to share honest feedback about products.

questions.explanation: "Inappropriate" is a vague standard, and the model is filling it in with "negative". The fix is to name the categories that justify removal and explicitly name the category that must NOT be removed (honest criticism). Stating both sides of the boundary is what reduces false positives while still catching real abuse.

whyWrong.B: A confidence instruction does not change what the model thinks "inappropriate" means; it will still be confident that harsh criticism is inappropriate.
whyWrong.C: This measures the wrong thing. Negativity is exactly what should be allowed, so filtering on it would remove even more honest reviews.
whyWrong.D: A persona is a mood, not a rule. It may shift tone slightly but gives no testable definition of what to remove and what to keep.

questions.mindset: Define what to remove AND what to keep; the 'keep' list is where false positives are fixed.

questions.scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration: years ago, an earlier model under-reported security issues, so someone added this line to the review prompt: "CRITICAL: You MUST flag EVERY possible security issue. Missing one is unacceptable." After the pipeline moved to a current Claude model, the reviewer now flags almost every string concatenation and every log statement as a possible injection or data leak.
questions.stem: The team wants the security findings to become precise again with the smallest prompt change and without missing real vulnerabilities. What should they do?

options.text: Keep the emphatic line and append "but do not flag false positives", so the model weighs the two pressures against each other.
Move the security check into a separate Claude call with the same instruction, so it does not crowd out the other review categories.
Switch back to the earlier model for the security category only, since its behavior matched the prompt the team wrote for it.
Replace the emphatic line with plain wording that spells out which security issues to report and when concatenation or logging is safe.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance notes that recent models are more responsive to the system prompt, so emphatic wording written to fix under-triggering on earlier models ("CRITICAL: You MUST...") can now cause over-triggering; the recommended fix is to dial the aggressive language back to normal wording. For precision, also replace the blanket rule with explicit criteria: which patterns are real vulnerabilities and which (constant strings, logs that contain no user data) are not.

whyWrong.A: Two vague, competing pressures leave the model to guess the trade-off from input to input; there is still no definition of a real issue.
whyWrong.B: Isolating the check does not change the instruction that causes the over-flagging; the separate call will produce the same noise.
whyWrong.C: Pinning an old model works around the prompt instead of fixing it, and gives up the newer model's improvements in every other respect.

questions.mindset: Shouting in the prompt over-triggers modern models; replace emphasis with a clear, calm criterion.

questions.scenario: Multi-Agent Research System: the web-search subagent is told to "keep only high-quality sources" before passing results to the synthesis subagent. Editors find that it keeps some anonymous blog posts while discarding a government statistics release because "it is a plain data table, not an analysis". Results also differ between runs on the same topic.
questions.stem: Which change to the search subagent's prompt will MOST effectively make source selection precise and consistent?

options.text: Tell the subagent to think harder about source quality and to explain in a sentence why each source it kept meets a high editorial standard.
Define qualifying sources by testable traits, such as primary data, peer review or a named publisher, and list source types to exclude.
Let the subagent keep every source it finds and ask the synthesis subagent to judge quality later, when it writes the report.
Add a second search subagent with the same prompt and keep only the sources that both subagents independently decide to keep.

questions.explanation: "High-quality" means different things on different runs, which explains both the wrong choices and the inconsistency. Turning it into checkable traits (primary data or peer review, an identifiable publisher, recency, excluded types such as anonymous opinion posts) gives the model a rule it can apply the same way every time and directly covers the government-statistics case.

whyWrong.A: Asking for more thought and a justification still leaves the "high editorial standard" undefined; the model will justify its own inconsistent idea of quality.
whyWrong.C: This moves the same vague judgment downstream and floods the synthesis subagent's context with low-value sources.
whyWrong.D: Two runs of the same vague prompt share the same blind spots; agreement between them does not make the standard correct and doubles the cost.

questions.mindset: Replace adjectives like 'high-quality' with traits the model can check.

questions.stem: A finance team uses Claude to flag employee expense reports for audit with the instruction "Flag anything suspicious." Claude flags about 35% of reports, but the auditors can only review about 5%, and most flags turn out to be fine. Policy has two kinds of rules: numeric ones (for example, any item over a set amount needs a receipt) and judgment ones (for example, the stated business purpose should fit the merchant and attendees). Which TWO changes will MOST effectively cut false flags while still catching real violations? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask Claude to attach a self-assessed suspicion score from 1 to 100 to each report and send only the reports above a cutoff tuned to auditor capacity.
Check the numeric rules, such as amount limits and missing receipts, in ordinary code before Claude sees the report, and pass it the results.
Change the instruction to "Flag only reports that are clearly and seriously suspicious" so that Claude applies a much higher bar.
Route reports to a larger model and ask it to double-check each of its own flags before it adds the report to the audit queue.
Give Claude explicit criteria for the judgment rules, such as when a purpose fits the merchant, and list common cases that are acceptable.

questions.explanation: Split the problem by rule type. Numeric policy is deterministic and well defined, so ordinary code should check it exactly and cheaply (Anthropic's guidance favors predefined code paths for well-defined tasks); asking a model to judge it only adds noise. For the rules that do need judgment, replace "suspicious" with explicit criteria, including normal cases that should not be flagged. Together these remove most false flags and keep real violations visible.

whyWrong.A: A self-assessed suspicion score is not calibrated to the policy, so tuning a cutoff to capacity drops real violations as readily as false ones.
whyWrong.C: Stronger adjectives do not define what is suspicious; the model still guesses, just with a different, unpredictable threshold.
whyWrong.D: A bigger model checking its own work still has no clear standard, and self-review tends to confirm earlier answers while adding cost.

questions.mindset: Put exact rules in code and give the model explicit criteria only for the parts that need judgment.

questions.stem: A team has rewritten the vague criteria in its PR-review prompt into explicit report and skip lists. Before switching the live pipeline to the new prompt, the engineering manager wants evidence that it is actually better and not just quieter. Which TWO steps give the MOST trustworthy evidence? Choose TWO.

options.text: Run both the old and new prompts on a set of past pull requests whose real issues and accepted patterns were already labeled by engineers.
Ask Claude to estimate the new prompt's precision by describing in its own words which findings it would now report and which it would skip.
Ship the new prompt to every repository at once and treat a falling count of posted comments over the next week as proof of improvement.
Compare how many false findings each prompt posts and how many engineer-confirmed real issues each misses, instead of counting posted findings.
Check that the new prompt handles the example diffs embedded in the prompt itself correctly, since those cover all of the key cases.

questions.explanation: Explicit criteria should be tested like any other change: run them on representative, labeled data and compare against the baseline. Measuring both precision (false findings) and recall (missed real issues) prevents a prompt that simply says less from looking like an improvement. Anthropic's evaluation guidance recommends task-specific test sets that reflect real inputs, including edge cases.

whyWrong.B: The model's description of its own behavior is not a measurement; only running it on labeled inputs shows what it actually does.
whyWrong.C: Fewer comments could mean real issues are now missed. A falling count says nothing about accuracy, and rolling out first exposes every team to the risk.
whyWrong.E: Testing on the prompt's own examples measures memorization, not how the criteria generalize to new pull requests.

questions.mindset: Precision gains only count if recall holds; measure both on labeled real data before rollout.

questions.scenario: Structured Data Extraction: a pipeline reads commercial leases and fills a `start_date` field that drives billing in the downstream finance system. The prompt says: "Extract the start date of the lease." Billing errors show that the model sometimes returns the signing date, sometimes the date the tenant may move in early for fit-out work, and sometimes a date from a referenced older agreement.
questions.stem: Which prompt change MOST directly fixes these wrong dates?

options.text: Tell the model that this field drives billing and that wrong dates are very costly, so it should take extra care before choosing.
Ask the model to return every date it finds in the lease, and let the finance team pick the right one when they review billing.
Ask the model to return null for `start_date` whenever the lease contains more than one date, so a person can review it.
Define the field as the date on which rent obligations begin, and state that signing, early-access and referenced-agreement dates do not count.

questions.explanation: The model is not careless; the instruction is ambiguous because a lease has several plausible "start" dates. A precise definition tied to the business meaning (when rent begins) plus explicit exclusions for the look-alike dates gives the model a test it can apply. Explaining why the field matters is useful context, but it does not resolve which date is meant.

whyWrong.A: Stressing importance does not tell the model which of several valid-looking dates you mean, so the same confusion remains.
whyWrong.B: This pushes the extraction work onto people and breaks the automated billing feed the pipeline exists to supply.
whyWrong.C: Almost every lease has several dates, so this would return null nearly always and turn the pipeline into manual review.

questions.mindset: Define the target field by its business meaning and name the look-alikes to ignore.

questions.scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent: the system prompt contains three example replies to show the desired tone. In all three, the customer had a delivery problem and the reply opens with a long apology and ends by offering a 10% discount code. Since the examples were added, the agent offers a discount code in nearly every conversation, including simple password resets and order-status questions.
questions.stem: What is the BEST way to keep the tone benefits of the examples while stopping the unwanted discount offers?

options.text: Rework the examples to cover varied request types, with most replies offering no compensation and one showing when a discount is warranted.
Add a line in capital letters saying discount codes must never be offered unless the customer explicitly asks for compensation.
Remove all three examples and describe the desired tone in a full paragraph of adjectives, so that no specific behavior gets copied by the model.
Add a post-processing filter that deletes any sentence containing a discount code from the reply before it is sent to the customer.

questions.explanation: Claude pays close attention to examples. Because every example shared the same incidental feature (a discount offer), the agent learned it as part of the pattern. Anthropic's guidance is to make examples diverse enough that the model does not pick up unintended patterns. Varying the request types, showing replies without compensation, and briefly explaining when a discount is appropriate keeps the tone signal and removes the accidental one.

whyWrong.B: An emphatic rule fights the examples instead of fixing them, and it overcorrects: it blocks discounts even in the delivery cases where policy allows them.
whyWrong.C: Dropping the examples throws away the most reliable way to steer tone; a list of adjectives will make tone less consistent.
whyWrong.D: Deleting sentences after generation leaves replies that promise something and then omit it, and does not address why the agent offers discounts.

questions.mindset: Whatever all your examples share, the model will copy; vary everything except what you want repeated.

questions.scenario: Structured Data Extraction: an invoice extractor's prompt contains two worked examples, each showing a short sample invoice followed by the JSON that should be produced. The examples and the real invoice are pasted one after another as plain text. Occasionally the output contains a vendor name or total that belongs to one of the sample invoices rather than the real one.
questions.stem: Which change MOST directly stops values from the examples leaking into real extractions?

options.text: Delete the examples and rely on the JSON schema alone, since the schema already lists every field the extractor needs to return.
Use sample invoices with obviously fake placeholder values, such as 'ACME TEST', so that any leaked values are easy to spot in later checks.
Wrap the samples in <example> tags inside <examples>, put the real invoice in its own tag, and say to extract only from that tag.
Move the examples to the very end of the prompt, after the real invoice, so they are read last and influence the output less.

questions.explanation: When examples and real input run together as plain text, the model can confuse which document it is supposed to extract from. Anthropic recommends wrapping examples in <example> tags (several in <examples>) so Claude can tell them apart from instructions and input, and putting each kind of content in its own tag. Pointing the instruction at the tagged input removes the ambiguity while keeping the examples' benefit.

whyWrong.A: A schema controls the shape of the output, not the judgment about values; removing the examples loses their accuracy and consistency benefits.
whyWrong.B: This makes the leak easier to detect but does nothing to prevent it; extractions would still fail, just more visibly.
whyWrong.D: Position alone does not tell the model which document is the real input; without clear boundaries the same confusion remains wherever the examples sit.

questions.mindset: Fence your examples off from the real input so the model always knows which is which.

questions.scenario: Structured Data Extraction: a shipping-document extractor must return `ship_date` in ISO 8601 format (YYYY-MM-DD), and the prompt says so clearly. The prompt also has four examples. Downstream validation shows that dates such as 03/04/2025 are sometimes written as 2025-03-04 and sometimes as 2025-04-03 for documents from the same European supplier. On review, one of the four examples converts a European day-first date as if it were month-first.
questions.stem: What should the team do FIRST?

options.text: Repeat the ISO 8601 rule in bold at the top and bottom of the prompt so the written instruction outweighs the examples.
Correct the faulty example, and make sure the examples show both day-first and month-first sources converted correctly.
Add a validator that rejects any converted date where the day is 12 or less, and send those documents to manual data entry instead.
Remove the date field from the examples entirely so the model follows only the written rule when it converts dates.

questions.explanation: Examples are a strong signal, and Claude follows them closely. When an example contradicts the instructions, the model gets mixed signals and the output becomes inconsistent. The first fix is to make the examples correct and to cover the hard case (day-first vs month-first sources) explicitly, so instructions and examples point the same way.

whyWrong.A: Repeating the rule does not remove the contradicting example, so the conflict and the inconsistency remain.
whyWrong.C: This sends every date in the first twelve days of a month to people, even correct ones, and still leaves the faulty example in place.
whyWrong.D: This removes the very case the examples should be teaching; the ambiguous day/month conversion is where examples help most.

questions.mindset: Audit your examples like code: a wrong example is a bug the model will faithfully reproduce.

questions.stem: A small operations team with no machine-learning background wants Claude to sort incoming supplier emails into five categories. Their first prompt has clear category definitions, but borderline emails are labeled inconsistently, so they plan to add few-shot examples. They have limited time. Which TWO practices will MOST improve the example set? Choose TWO.

options.text: Write about twenty examples for the most common category, so the model sees plenty of the emails it will receive most often.
Write short, idealized emails with perfect spelling and one clear topic each, so every example demonstrates its category cleanly.
Ask Claude to review the draft set for relevance and diversity and to suggest more examples, then check them before use.
Paste the examples as plain paragraphs after the category definitions, with no tags around them, so they read as part of the instructions.
Base examples on real, anonymized emails, including borderline ones that mention two topics, with the reason for each label.

questions.explanation: Good examples are relevant (they mirror real inputs), diverse (they cover edge cases) and targeted at the ambiguity that causes errors. Real anonymized emails, including the two-topic borderline ones with a one-line reason, teach the boundary. Anthropic also suggests asking Claude to evaluate examples for relevance and diversity or to generate more from an initial set, which saves time; a person should still check the results.

whyWrong.A: Piling up examples of the easy, common case does not teach the borderline judgments and can bias the model toward that category.
whyWrong.B: Idealized examples do not look like real inbox traffic and skip exactly the messy, mixed cases that are being mislabeled.
whyWrong.D: Examples that blur into the instructions are harder for the model to tell apart from the rules; the docs recommend wrapping each in <example> tags (inside <examples>) so Claude can distinguish them.

questions.mindset: Pick examples from real, messy inputs at the boundary, and use Claude to help widen and critique the set.

questions.stem: After adding four few-shot examples to a ticket-routing prompt, an analyst reports "100% accuracy" and asks to ship it. You learn she tested the prompt on the same four tickets used as the examples. What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.text: Approve the change, because a perfect score on the example tickets shows the model has learned the routing logic they demonstrate.
Ask her to rerun the same four example tickets several more times, to confirm the result is stable before the change ships.
Ask her to add more examples until the prompt contains every possible routing case, so that no real ticket is ever unfamiliar.
Ask her to measure performance on a separate set of real tickets that were not used as examples, including borderline ones, before shipping.

questions.explanation: A model that sees the exact answer in its prompt will usually reproduce it, so scoring on the examples says nothing about new tickets. The meaningful test is a held-out set of representative tickets, including the borderline cases the examples were meant to fix, compared against the previous prompt.

whyWrong.A: A perfect score on inputs whose answers are in the prompt measures copying, not whether the routing logic generalizes.
whyWrong.B: Repeating the same flawed test only confirms the model can copy consistently; it still says nothing about unseen tickets.
whyWrong.C: Real tickets vary without limit, so a prompt cannot list every case; examples are meant to teach patterns that generalize, and that still needs held-out testing.

questions.mindset: Never grade a prompt on the examples it contains; test on held-out real inputs.

questions.stem: Over a year, a classification prompt has grown to 40 few-shot examples because each new failure got its own example. The prompt now accounts for most of the per-request cost and noticeably slows responses. Many examples are near-duplicates of each other, and the instructions and examples rarely change between requests. The team wants the lowest cost and latency without losing consistency. Which TWO actions are MOST appropriate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Cut the set to a few diverse examples that cover the real decision boundaries, and confirm on a held-out set that accuracy holds.
Remove all the examples and replace them with a much longer written description of each category, because plain text is cheaper than examples.
Use prompt caching on the unchanging instructions and examples at the start of the prompt, so repeated requests reuse that prefix.
Keep all 40 examples and switch to a larger model, so the longer prompt is processed with better attention to every example.
Split the 40 examples across four parallel calls with ten examples each, and take a majority vote on the final label they produce.

questions.explanation: Few-shot works best with a small number of well-chosen, diverse examples (Anthropic suggests 3-5 as a starting point); dozens of near-duplicates add cost without adding new information. After pruning, verify on held-out data that nothing regressed. Because the instructions and examples form a stable prefix, prompt caching cuts the cost and latency of reprocessing it on every request.

whyWrong.B: Descriptions alone were already failing on these cases; dropping every example throws away the main source of consistency.
whyWrong.D: A larger model makes each request cost more and does nothing about the redundant examples driving cost and latency.
whyWrong.E: Four calls per request multiply cost, and each call sees only part of the boundary coverage, which can make results less consistent.

questions.mindset: A few well-chosen examples beat a pile of near-duplicates; cache what does not change.

questions.stem: A marketing team uses Claude to draft product announcements, social posts and newsletter blurbs. The prompt describes the brand voice as "warm, confident, plain-spoken, never salesy", yet drafts swing between stiff corporate language and over-excited hype. The team has a library of approved past pieces. What is the MOST effective next step?

options.text: Add three or four approved pieces, one per content type, as tagged examples of the brand voice next to the existing description.
Expand the voice description into a full page of adjectives and banned words, so that every aspect of the tone is spelled out clearly.
Tell Claude to write in the style of a well-known copywriter whose tone the team admires and believes matches the brand's voice.
Generate five separate drafts for every request and have a team member pick whichever one sounds closest to the brand voice.

questions.explanation: Tone is hard to pin down with adjectives, which is why the drafts swing. Anthropic notes that examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer format, tone and structure. A few approved pieces spanning the different content types show the voice directly and vary enough that Claude learns the tone rather than one format.

whyWrong.B: More adjectives give more room for interpretation; the issue is that descriptions of tone are vague, not that there are too few of them.
whyWrong.C: An outside writer's style is not the brand's voice and may conflict with it; it replaces one vague target with another.
whyWrong.D: This multiplies cost and human effort for every request while leaving the underlying inconsistency unsolved.

questions.mindset: When words can't pin down a style, show it with a few varied examples.
